title: PAUL BEGGED GOD THREE TIMES TO TAKE AWAY HIS THORN. GOD SAID NO. AND THE REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN SUFFERING.
paragraphs: PAUL BEGGED GOD THREE TIMES TO TAKE AWAY HIS THORN. GOD SAID NO. AND THE REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN SUFFERING.
What if the prayer God hasn't answered is not proof that He has abandoned you—but the very place where Christ is teaching you that His grace can hold you when your strength cannot?
There is a kind of pain that makes even the strongest believer whisper questions they are afraid to say out loud.
“Lord, how much longer?”
“Have I not suffered enough?”
“Why am I still fighting something I have begged You to remove?”
And perhaps the most heartbreaking question of all…
“God, if You really love me, why won't You take this away?”
You prayed.
You fasted.
You cried until there were no tears left.
You confessed your sins. You searched your heart. You opened your Bible, looking for an answer. You listened to sermons about breakthrough, healing, deliverance, and victory.
And yet, when morning came, the pain was still there.
The diagnosis hadn't changed.
The temptation hadn't disappeared.
The grief still followed you into quiet rooms.
The anxiety still pressed against your chest.
The person you loved was still gone.
The battle you thought would end months ago was still waiting for you when you opened your eyes.
And somewhere between another unanswered prayer and another exhausted night, a terrible thought entered your mind.
“Maybe God is disappointed in me.”
But before you accept that thought as truth, you need to hear what happened to one of the most faithful servants of Jesus Christ.
Because the apostle Paul knew what it meant to pray desperately and not receive the answer he wanted.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And the Lord's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
It was something Paul would eventually treasure more than the strength he had been asking for.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Read that again.
God did not tell Paul that his suffering was imaginary.
He did not accuse him of lacking faith because he wanted relief.
He did not tell him to pretend the thorn wasn't painful.
Instead, Christ met him in the very weakness Paul wanted to escape.
And that changes everything.
Because sometimes the greatest testimony is not that God removed what was hurting you.
Sometimes the testimony is that Jesus held you while it was still hurting.
Paul was not an ordinary man living an ordinary Christian life.
He had encountered the risen Christ.

He had preached the Gospel across cities and nations. He had endured persecution, imprisonment, beatings, shipwrecks, betrayal, hunger, sleepless nights, and danger from people who wanted him silenced.
He had witnessed the transforming power of the Gospel.
He had seen doors open where there appeared to be no way forward.
He had experienced extraordinary revelations from God.
And yet, in 2 Corinthians 12, this same apostle reveals something deeply personal.
Something humiliating.
Something painful.
Something he could not overcome by determination, experience, or spiritual maturity.
He called it a thorn.
The Greek text describes it as σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί (skolops tē sarki), commonly translated “a thorn in the flesh.”
The word skolops can refer to a thorn or pointed stake. The expression communicates something painfully piercing or afflicting, not merely a minor inconvenience.
Paul writes:
Notice the tension.
Paul describes the affliction as a messenger of Satan, yet he also recognizes that God was accomplishing a purpose through what he suffered.
This does not mean Satan was good.
It does not mean evil suddenly became holy.
It means that even the adversary's hostility could not place Paul's life outside God's sovereign authority.
What was meant to afflict him would not be permitted to have the final word over him.
And the purpose Paul identifies is astonishing.
To keep him from becoming conceited because of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
Think about that.
The man who had been entrusted with remarkable spiritual experiences still needed the humility of dependence.
Paul had seen things that could have made him proud.
But he was learning that revelation without humility could become dangerous.
A person can know much about God and still need to learn how desperately he depends on God.
A person can preach grace to thousands and still need grace to survive the night.
A person can lead others toward Christ and still carry a private struggle nobody sees.
Perhaps that is the part of Paul's story that touches you most.
Because people may know your ministry but not your misery.
They may admire your faith without understanding your fatigue.
They may see your Sunday worship but never hear your Monday crying.
They may call you strong because they have never watched you collapse when the door closes.
And perhaps you have become so skilled at encouraging everyone else that nobody realizes how desperately you need encouragement yourself.
Paul understood something of that contradiction.
He was an apostle.
And he was afflicted.
He was called.
And he was weak.
He belonged to Christ.
And he still needed help.
Your suffering does not automatically disqualify your calling.
Your weakness does not automatically cancel your usefulness.
Your tears do not make your faith counterfeit.
The Bible never promises that faithful Christians will be spared every painful circumstance in this present life.
In fact, Jesus told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not promise a world without trouble.
He promised that trouble would not overturn His victory.
And sometimes we confuse those two things.
We think victory means never hurting again.
But biblical victory begins with belonging to the risen Christ, who has overcome sin and death, even while we await the fullness of His restoration.
Paul understood suffering.
But he did not enjoy it.
He prayed for relief.
“For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:8, KJV
The Greek says:
ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν κύριον παρεκάλεσα ἵνα ἀποστῇ ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ
Hyper toutou tris ton kyrion parekalesa hina apostē ap' emou.
A faithful rendering is:
“Concerning this, three times I pleaded with the Lord that it might depart from me.”
The verb parekalesa, from parakaleō, carries the sense of appealing, urging, or earnestly asking.
Paul was not casually mentioning an inconvenience.
He was pleading.
He wanted it gone.
And Scripture records three appeals.
We are not told how far apart those appeals occurred or exactly what each occasion looked like.
But we are told enough to understand that Paul sought relief earnestly.
That matters.
Because there are Christians who have been made to feel ashamed for asking God to end their suffering.
As though requesting healing were a failure of surrender.
As though crying for deliverance meant they had not matured spiritually.
As though genuine faith could only say, “Lord, let it continue.”
But Paul asked for the thorn to leave.
And Jesus Himself, in Gethsemane, prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39, KJV
The suffering of Jesus was unique. He was approaching the cross, where He would bear the sins of His people. Paul's affliction was not the same as Christ's redemptive suffering.
But Gethsemane teaches us something precious about prayer.
Honest anguish and genuine submission are not enemies.
You can ask God to change your circumstances while trusting Him with the outcome.
You can cry for healing and still love the Healer.
You can pray for deliverance without demanding that God obey your timetable.
You can say, “Father, I do not want this,” and still say, “Your will be done.”
And perhaps somebody reading this needs permission to stop pretending.
You do not have to dress your grief in religious language before bringing it to God.
He already knows.
He knows what you whisper into your pillow.
He knows what you cannot explain to your family.
He knows the struggle behind your smile.
He knows the temptation you are ashamed to confess.
He knows the exhaustion you hide because everybody expects you to be strong.
You can bring all of it into His presence.
Not because every desire of your heart is automatically righteous.
Not because every interpretation you have of your suffering is correct.
But because the throne of grace is open to those who come through Jesus Christ.
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” — Hebrews 4:16, KJV
And then comes the answer that has comforted suffering believers for centuries.
“And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
The original Greek is especially beautiful:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου, ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται.
Arkei soi hē charis mou, hē gar dynamis en astheneia teleitai.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for power is brought to its intended fullness in weakness.”
The Greek word ἀρκεῖ (arkei) means “is sufficient” or “is enough.”
χάρις (charis) means “grace.”
δύναμις (dynamis) means “power.”
And ἀσθένεια (astheneia) means “weakness,” a word that can encompass frailty, limitation, or incapacity.
The verb τελεῖται (teleitai) communicates being completed, accomplished, or brought to its intended goal.
Christ's power was not deficient and waiting for Paul's suffering to improve it.
Rather, Christ's already-perfect power would be displayed fully through Paul's weakness.
Do you see the difference?
God was not telling Paul that weakness was stronger than divine power.
He was telling him that divine power did not depend on human strength.
Paul did not have to become invulnerable before Christ could work through him.
He did not have to escape every limitation before his life could glorify God.
The grace of Jesus was enough to sustain him in the calling Christ had given him.
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not say every illness, trauma, disability, or hardship has been personally assigned by God to teach us humility.
Paul identifies a particular purpose for his particular affliction.
We should not presume to know the hidden reason behind someone else's suffering.
And we should never use Paul's thorn to discourage medical treatment, counseling, practical assistance, protection from abuse, or continued prayer for healing.
God's grace can sustain believers through suffering, and His provision may include physicians, medicine, wise counselors, faithful friends, and the care of the church.
The lesson is not that you must remain in every painful circumstance.
The lesson is that when relief has not yet come, the grace of Christ has not become powerless.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have been waiting for the wrong evidence that God is near.
We thought His presence would be proven when the problem disappeared.
When the marriage was restored.
When the test results came back clear.
When the bills were paid.
When the nightmares stopped.
When the addiction no longer tempted us.
When the grief no longer interrupted ordinary days.
And we began measuring God's love by how quickly our circumstances improved.
But the cross will not allow us to measure divine love that way.
At Calvary, the beloved Son of God suffered.
Not because the Father had ceased to love Him.
Not because Jesus had failed.
But because, according to God's saving purpose, the sinless Savior was giving His life for sinners.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
The clearest proof of God's love is not the absence of suffering.
It is Jesus Christ crucified and risen for our salvation.
That truth does not answer every question about why God permits particular sorrows.
But it tells us where to look when suffering tempts us to doubt His heart.
Look to the cross.
Look to the Savior whose hands were pierced.
Look to the empty tomb.
Look to the One who did not merely speak about suffering from a safe distance but entered our broken world and conquered death.
Paul's thorn points us toward dependence on Christ.
But Christ's wounds point us toward redemption.
And there is an enormous difference between those two things.
Paul could not save himself through suffering.
Neither can you.
Your pain does not purchase forgiveness.
Your endurance does not pay for your sins.
Your tears do not make you worthy of heaven.
Only Jesus saves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
This is where the Gospel breaks through our obsession with proving ourselves.
You cannot impress God into loving you.
You cannot suffer enough to earn His acceptance.
You cannot manufacture spiritual strength that makes you independent of His mercy.
Salvation is not a reward for the unbroken.
It is God's gift to sinners who trust in Jesus Christ.
And that includes the ashamed.
The exhausted.
The repentant.
The person who fell again after promising never to fall.
The believer who is tired of fighting a hidden battle.
The one who has spent years looking respectable while carrying guilt that feels unbearable.
Consider Paul himself.
Before he became a messenger of Christ, he was Saul, a persecutor of the church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He pursued believers.
He sought to destroy the very community he would later serve.
His past was not a harmless misunderstanding.
It involved real sin and real harm.
Yet the risen Jesus confronted him.
And the persecutor became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
Paul later wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
And then he explained why mercy had been shown to him: so that Jesus Christ might demonstrate His longsuffering as an example to those who would believe in Him for everlasting life.
What a testimony.
The man who once hunted Christians became a servant of the Christ he had opposed.
But even after his conversion, even after years of ministry, even after extraordinary revelations, Paul still lived by grace.
Not yesterday's grace alone.
Not the grace that first rescued him alone.
Daily grace.
Sustaining grace.
Grace sufficient for the weakness he could not remove.
That is the Gospel.
Grace is not merely the doorway into the Christian life.
It is the ground on which believers continue to stand.
And that means your story is not finished simply because you are still struggling.
Your past does not have to dictate your future.
Your sin must be confronted, not excused.
Your wounds may need care, not concealment.
Your relationships may require repentance, restitution, boundaries, and patient rebuilding.
But none of those realities place a repentant sinner beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not promise that every consequence of your past disappears.
It promises something infinitely greater: forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life in Christ.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
And now we arrive at the part of Paul's testimony that is almost impossible to understand until you have lived long enough to know what weakness feels like.
After Christ answered him, Paul wrote:
“Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
And then:
“For when I am weak, then am I strong.” — 2 Corinthians 12:10, KJV
Paul was not celebrating pain for its own sake.
He was celebrating the sufficiency of Christ.
He was not saying that suffering was pleasant.
He was saying that suffering could not separate him from the power of the Savior.
The Greek expression translated “may rest upon me” uses ἐπισκηνώσῃ (episkēnōsē), a verb associated with dwelling or pitching a tent over someone.
It paints a remarkable picture.
Paul's weakness becomes the setting in which Christ's power rests upon him.
Not because Paul has finally become impressive.
But because he has learned that he does not need to be.
Imagine spending your entire life trying to be strong enough that nobody notices you are struggling.
Imagine believing that your value depends on always having the right answer.
Always keeping the family together.
Always paying the bills.
Always encouraging others.
Always winning.
Always appearing spiritually victorious.
And then imagine discovering that Jesus never asked you to become your own savior.
He asked you to follow Him.
To trust Him.
To abide in Him.
To receive what you cannot manufacture.
To obey Him even when obedience costs you.
To depend on His grace when your resources run dry.
Some of us are exhausted not only because life is difficult, but because we have been carrying the impossible burden of pretending we are sufficient without Christ.
And the Gospel confronts that illusion.
Jesus says:
“For without me ye can do nothing.” — John 15:5, KJV
Nothing of lasting spiritual fruit can be produced apart from Him.
Not by charisma.
Not by religious performance.
Not by popularity.
Not by pretending we never struggle.
And this is why Paul's testimony is so liberating.
He did not need the thorn to disappear before he could testify about the faithfulness of Jesus.
His testimony existed in the middle of the struggle.
Perhaps yours does too.
Maybe you cannot yet say, “God healed me.”
But you can truthfully say, “God has sustained me.”
Maybe you cannot say, “My family has been restored.”
But you can say, “Jesus is teaching me to walk in truth, forgiveness, and wisdom.”
Maybe you cannot say, “The temptation is gone.”
But you can say, “By God's grace, I am learning to resist, confess, seek help, and refuse to make peace with sin.”
Maybe you cannot say, “I no longer grieve.”
But you can say, “I grieve with hope because Christ has risen.”
Those are not insignificant testimonies.
They are evidence that the Gospel reaches into real human lives.
But there is something else we need to understand.
Paul's thorn is not permission to remain comfortable in deliberate sin.
Some people use the language of weakness to excuse behavior Scripture commands them to repent of.
They say, “This is just my thorn,” when what they mean is, “I do not want to surrender this sin.”
But a sinful habit we are called to put to death must not be confused with an affliction Paul pleaded for God to remove.
The Bible tells believers to resist temptation, flee sexual immorality, put away falsehood, turn from bitterness, and walk by the Spirit.
God's grace is not a license to keep sinning without repentance.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace also trains us to reject ungodliness.
If your hidden struggle involves sin, the answer is not to rename it as your destiny.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it to God.
Seek trustworthy accountability where needed.
Turn away from what is destroying your soul.
Trust Christ for mercy and transformation.
And if you have fallen, do not turn your failure into a reason to run farther from the Savior.
Run to Him in repentance.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
Not because sin is small.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
And if your suffering is not the result of your own wrongdoing, do not allow anyone to burden you with accusations God has not made.
The disciples once encountered a man born blind and asked Jesus whose sin had caused his condition.
Jesus rejected their assumption that his blindness was the direct consequence of his sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1–3).
We must learn the difference between biblical conviction and careless condemnation.
Not every wound is punishment.
Not every unanswered prayer is rejection.
Not every delayed healing reveals deficient faith.
And not every hardship comes with an explanation we can discover in this life.
Sometimes the most faithful sentence we can speak is simply:
“Lord, I do not understand. But I know You are worthy of my trust.”
That is not the absence of faith.
It can be an expression of faith struggling honestly in the presence of God.
And perhaps right now, you are standing in that very place.
Between what you asked for and what God has permitted.
Between the miracle you hoped to see and the endurance you never wanted to need.
Between the person you used to be and the person Christ is shaping you to become.
You have questions.
You have scars.
You may even have anger that you need to bring honestly before God rather than hide behind a religious smile.
And still, the invitation of Jesus remains.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
He does not say, “Come only when you are no longer exhausted.”
He does not say, “Come only after you have solved everything.”
He calls the burdened.
He calls the weary.
He calls sinners to repentance and faith.
He calls His people to continue trusting Him.
And He gives rest that is deeper than the illusion of a trouble-free life.
If you have been waiting to return to Jesus until you feel worthy, you have misunderstood grace.
Come because you need Him.
Come confessing your sin.
Come trusting His finished work on the cross and His resurrection from the dead.
Come willing to follow Him.
And if you already belong to Christ but have grown weary, remember that His faithfulness is not exhausted by your limitations.
His grace has not run out because your strength has.
This is why I want to ask you something deeply personal.
What is the thorn you keep praying about?
Not necessarily something you need to reveal publicly in detail.
Some wounds deserve privacy. Some struggles require professional help and the protection of trusted people.
But in your own heart, before God, can you name what has been weighing on you?
Is it grief?
A physical limitation?
A long season of waiting?
A battle with fear?
The shame of your past?
A burden you have been carrying alone?
Or perhaps your deepest struggle is the fear that God has forgotten you.
Not as a performance.
Not as a promise that you will never stumble.
But as a simple confession that you still want to cling to Jesus.
Your words might remind another weary believer that they are not the only person struggling to trust God.
Think about that friend who always says, “I'm fine,” even though you know life has been hard.
Think about the family member who has quietly withdrawn from fellowship.
Think about the believer who is questioning whether God still hears their prayers.
Think about the person who has not yet understood the grace offered through Jesus Christ.
Send this article to them.
You never know who might be reading your post in silence.
Someone may be searching for the courage to pray again.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible.
Someone may be one conversation away from seeking help.
Someone may be ready to hear the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to know every detail of their story to share the truth that changed yours.
Not because these words possess any special power.
But because the Scriptures they point toward remain true even when your emotions fluctuate.
Return to 2 Corinthians 12.
Read it in its context.
Remember Paul's plea.
Remember Christ's answer.
Remember that grace is not measured by the absence of pain.
And remember that the Savior who sustained Paul is the same risen Lord believers worship today.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to substitute online content for the preaching of God's Word, fellowship, prayer, pastoral care, and discipleship in a faithful Christian community.
But to serve as another place where people can encounter Scripture, be encouraged toward repentance and faith, grow in biblical understanding, and find resources that point them back to Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to encourage serious study, spiritual maturity, and a life shaped by the Gospel.
And if these articles and resources have helped you, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading.
Not because your salvation, spiritual standing, or God's favor depends on financial support.
Christ has already accomplished what money could never purchase.
But because the work of sharing biblical teaching, preparing discipleship resources, and reaching people with the message of Jesus requires real time, effort, and support.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
If you already give tithes or offerings as part of your Christian stewardship, we encourage you to honor those commitments prayerfully.
If you are unable to give financially, you are no less welcome here.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
Jesus is the reason.
There is room here for the person who has walked with Jesus for decades and for the person who is opening the Bible with serious questions for the first time.
Our desire is that every article, every resource, and every conversation will ultimately point beyond Gospel Warrior to the One who alone can save.
Jesus Christ.
Because a ministry is not the Savior.
A library is not the source of eternal life.
Christ is.
And if this ministry ever becomes more important than the Lord it proclaims, it has lost its purpose.
So please hear the heart behind this invitation.
Follow along because growing in biblical truth is worth your time.
But worship Jesus.
Trust Jesus.
Obey Jesus.
Give glory to Jesus.
Always.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought you here.
Why did God say no when Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed?
The text does not record the Lord saying the single word “no.” It records something richer: Christ answered Paul by declaring that His grace was sufficient and His power was made perfect in weakness.
The affliction was not removed in the account.
Paul was given something he needed to understand about the power of Christ.
The thorn humbled him.
It kept him dependent.
And it became the setting in which Christ's sufficiency was displayed.
That is what Scripture explicitly teaches.
But here is what we must never forget.
Paul's particular explanation is not a universal formula for diagnosing every unanswered prayer.
We do not always know why a burden remains.
We do not always see what God is doing.
And faith does not require us to invent explanations when Scripture has not given them.
Sometimes God heals.
Sometimes He delivers.
Sometimes He opens a door we thought was permanently closed.
Sometimes He sustains us through a long season we would never have chosen.
And every believer still waits for the final redemption of the body and the day when Christ will make all things new.
The Christian hope is not that pain will always remain.
It is that pain will not remain forever.
Revelation 21:4 promises a day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is where the story of suffering believers is heading.
Not toward an endless thorn.
Toward resurrection.
Toward the presence of God.
Toward the complete victory of Jesus Christ.
Paul's thorn did not have the last word.
And neither will yours.
So tonight, if you find yourself praying the same prayer again, do not assume that repetition makes you a failure.
Keep coming to the Father through Jesus.
Ask for healing.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask for deliverance.
Seek the help you need.
Confess the sins you must forsake.
Receive the support of faithful believers.
And entrust the outcome to the Lord whose wisdom is greater than yours and whose love has been revealed at the cross.
You may not have the explanation you wanted.
You may not yet have the relief you requested.
But if you belong to Christ, you have a Savior who will not abandon you.
And perhaps your prayer tonight will sound different.
Not because you have stopped asking for the thorn to be removed.
But because you are beginning to understand that your life is held by Someone stronger than the thorn.

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have been carrying. You know the prayers I have repeated and the answers I still do not understand. Forgive my sins. Correct what needs to change in me. Heal what You will, deliver me from evil, and give me wisdom to seek the help I need. Teach me to trust Your Word when my feelings are overwhelmed. Let Your power be seen in my weakness. Keep my heart near You, and let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen.”
Not with a promise that their suffering will disappear tomorrow.
But with the truth that the risen Christ remains worthy of their trust today.
Because the most unforgettable part of Paul's story is not that he had a thorn.
It is that, even with the thorn, he belonged to Jesus.
And that is the truth I want you to carry with you long after you close this page.
The thorn may still be there when you wake up tomorrow—but so will the grace of the Savior who has promised never to leave His own.
